chapters.title: Chapter 2: Who Needs to Pay Advance Tax

body.text: Freelancers and self-employed professionals are the people advance tax was built for: income arrives without a payroll, often without TDS, and in amounts that swing month to month. Presumptive taxation makes their life simpler in two ways. It lets them declare a fixed share of receipts as profit, and it lets them pay all their advance tax in one instalment by 15 March.

children.text: India's freelance economy runs on UPI, Payoneer and Skydo transfers, not payslips. A developer in Bengaluru billing a US startup, a Jaipur seller running an Instagram store, and a Lucknow doctor consulting at three hospitals all face the same question every year: how much tax do I owe, and when? This lesson answers both, and shows how differently TDS treats them.
Who Deducts TDS on a Freelancer's Income?

Whether TDS reduces your advance tax depends almost entirely on who your clients are. Section 393 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old sections 193 to 194T) requires many Indian businesses to deduct TDS on fees they pay. Individuals paying for personal work usually do not, and foreign clients never deduct Indian TDS.

markDefs.definition: A scheme where eligible small businesses and professionals declare income as a fixed percentage of turnover or gross receipts, instead of computing actual profit from detailed books of account.

children.text: Keeping full accounts, tracking every expense and getting books audited is a burden for a one-person business.
lets eligible taxpayers skip it. The old Act spread the scheme across sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE. The 2025 Act consolidates all three into section 58, with the same limits and rates.

stats.label: Professionals: deemed profit

stats.label: Small businesses: deemed profit

body.caption: You may declare more than 50%, but not less, unless you keep books and get them audited

children.text: The professional scheme is open only to residents in specified professions: legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, company secretaries, information technology, film artists and a few other notified professions. A content writer, a social media manager or a fitness coach generally cannot use it, though they may be able to use the business scheme if their activity is treated as a business.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Professional's Deemed Profit
body.textWithBlank: Under the presumptive scheme for specified professionals, income is taken as at least ___% of gross receipts.
body.explanation: Specified professionals with receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh where cash receipts are 5% or less, can declare 50% of gross receipts as income. The other half is treated as covering expenses, whatever they actually were.

children.text: Three Freelancers, Three Very Different Outcomes

Sameera is a freelance software developer in Bengaluru. Her ₹36,00,000 of receipts for tax year 2026-27 come entirely from two US clients, paid digitally, with no Indian TDS. Her actual expenses on a laptop, co-working space and software are about ₹6,00,000.

body.title: Sameera's tax on ₹36,00,000 of receipts, new regime

columns.label: Presumptive scheme (50%)
points: No detailed books or audit required
Pay all advance tax by 15 March

columns.label: Regular books of account
points: Must maintain books and track every expense

body.label: Sameera's saving from the presumptive scheme
body.context: Because her real expenses are well below 50% of receipts. Her whole tax of ₹1,66,400 is uncovered by TDS, so it is all advance tax, due in full by 15 March 2027.

children.text: Dr Anand is a consultant physician in Lucknow who visits three private hospitals. His receipts are ₹40,00,000, and every hospital deducts TDS at 10%, a total of ₹4,00,000. Under the presumptive scheme his income is ₹20,00,000 and his tax is ₹2,08,000. His TDS already exceeds his tax by ₹1,92,000. He owes no advance tax at all, and will get a refund when he files.

Farida runs an online store in Jaipur selling handmade candles through Instagram and her own website. Her turnover is ₹2.5 crore, all received digitally, so she can use the business scheme at 6%. Her presumptive income is ₹15,00,000 and her tax is ₹1,09,200, with no TDS from her retail customers. Like Sameera, she is liable for advance tax and can pay it in one instalment by 15 March.

body.title: Quick Check: One Instalment
body.question: Sameera declares income under the presumptive scheme for professionals. By when must she have paid her advance tax for tax year 2026-27 to avoid interest for deferring instalments?
options: 15% by 15 June 2026, then 45%, 75% and 100% by the usual dates
Nothing until she files her return, because presumptive taxpayers are exempt from advance tax
body.explanation: Taxpayers who declare income under the presumptive schemes may pay the whole of their advance tax in a single instalment by 15 March. They are not exempt from advance tax, and paying on 31 March would still be advance tax but attracts interest for the short instalment on 15 March.

body.title: Try It: Kavya's Design Studio
body.prompt: Kavya is an interior designer in Hyderabad. Her gross receipts for tax year 2026-27 are ₹44 lakh, all received by bank transfer from individual homeowners who deduct no TDS. She uses the presumptive scheme for professionals and the new regime. Including 4% cess, what is her advance tax due by 15 March 2027? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Presumptive income is 50% of ₹44,00,000, which is ₹22,00,000. Slab tax is ₹20,000 plus ₹40,000 plus ₹60,000 plus ₹80,000 on the first ₹20 lakh, and 25% of ₹2,00,000 (₹50,000), totalling ₹2,50,000. With 4% cess, tax is ₹2,60,000. With no TDS, all of it is advance tax, payable by 15 March 2027.

body.title: Tax for a professional under the 50% scheme with no TDS, new regime

children.text: Up to ₹24 lakh of receipts, the rebate means a presumptive professional pays no tax. Above that, tax climbs quickly, and because none of it is deducted at source, all of it lands on the single 15 March due date.
The Single Instalment Is Not a Savings Plan

body.text: Being allowed to pay everything by 15 March does not mean you should wait. A freelancer who owes ₹2,60,000 on 15 March and has not set it aside faces a real cash crunch in the year's busiest month for tax. Many presumptive taxpayers deliberately pay in quarterly chunks anyway. Early payments are always credited, and nothing is lost by paying before the deadline.

body.title: Sameera's year: a disciplined presumptive taxpayer

body.text: The business scheme has a lock-in that the professional scheme does not. A business that opts for it and then drops out in a later year, by declaring lower profit, generally cannot use it again for the next five years. Professionals under the 50% scheme do not face this restriction, but should still choose deliberately rather than switching every year.

body.title: Scenario: The Architect Who Grew Too Fast
body.scenario: Rohan is an architect in Delhi, a resident, paid entirely by bank transfer. In June 2026 he expects receipts of about ₹70 lakh for the year and plans to use the presumptive scheme for professionals, paying all advance tax by 15 March 2027. He pays nothing in June, September or December. In February 2027 two large projects close early, and his receipts for the year reach ₹82 lakh.
body.prompt: Can Rohan still use the presumptive scheme and the single 15 March instalment? What does the change mean for his advance tax, and what should he do now?
body.modelAnswer: No. The professional scheme applies only up to ₹75 lakh of gross receipts where cash receipts are 5% or less, and Rohan has crossed it. His income will have to be computed from actual books of account, and at this level of receipts a tax audit will generally also apply. Because he is no longer declaring presumptive income, the single-instalment facility falls away, and the regular cumulative schedule of 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% applies. Since he paid nothing by June, September or December, interest for deferment of those instalments is likely to be charged under section 425. He should immediately estimate actual profit from his books, pay the full estimated advance tax by 15 March 2027 to stop further interest, and get his accountant to set up proper books and an audit for the year. The lesson for any growing freelancer: recheck eligibility every quarter, not just in June.

body.title: Set Up Your Year
steps: Check whether your work falls in a specified profession under the 50% scheme, or is a business eligible for the 6% or 8% scheme
Estimate gross receipts for the year and confirm you will stay within the limit, and that cash receipts will stay at 5% or less if you rely on the higher limit
List clients by type: Indian companies that deduct TDS, individuals who do not, and foreign clients who never do
Check AIS each quarter for TDS deducted by Indian clients, and compare it with your estimated tax
Set aside a fixed percentage of every receipt for tax, even if your deadline is 15 March
Keep bank statements, invoices and foreign inward remittance certificates, since the return still has to be backed by records of receipts

body.description: Pay advance tax through e-Pay Tax, check TDS from Indian clients in AIS, and file your return declaring presumptive income.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 sections in brackets. Examples use new regime rates for tax year 2026-27, ignore GST and surcharge, and reflect the position as understood at the time of writing. Eligibility for presumptive taxation depends on the nature of your work. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
